author: Colorado Wealth Management Fund
title: Retiring With Higher Yields
text:
This research report was produced by The REIT Forum with assistance from Big Dog Investments .
Whether you recently entered retirement or are planning to do so, you may be hunting for solid dividend stocks.
That hunt will most likely lead you to REITs. REITs are a great investment. They benefit from having no corporate taxes.
Yes, the dividends are taxed at higher rates, but the benefit of no corporate taxes is more important.
The REIT dividends also received a potential tax break in the recent tax reform . The basics of it is they reduced taxes on the dividend.
Consequently, REITs remain a very attractive investment for both retirees and those planning to retire at some point.
Picking the right REITs Many investors focus only on the dividend yield when evaluating REITs. Some, go a step further and look at FFO or AFFO. That is a step in the right direction.
Ideally, investors should also be looking at the level of operating expenses and the leverage of the REIT.
Where the dividend counts The dividend yield is one important metric, but it should not be the only metric investors are looking at. The dividend often falls after the other fundamentals fall apart. Because management can sustain the dividend temporarily, even as the company fails, it is unwise to buy the yield without researching the stock.
The most important historical data about the dividend is the growth history. A dividend that is growing even slightly is a much better sign than a dividend that is flat. If management of a REIT is struggling, they will often attempt to hold the dividend steady. When the REIT is struggling, you will rarely see dividend increases.
Small dividend raises Even a tiny bump in the dividend is perfectly acceptable. Investors shouldn’t focus too heavily on the rate of dividend growth. Extremely high rates of growth can not be sustained. They should not be used to project the future rate of dividend growth. It is more important that the REIT be consistently growing the dividend.
For instance, Realty Income Corporation ( O ) and National Retail Properties ( NNN ) have decades of consistent dividend increases. This is a clear sign of the strength of the business model.
FFO and AFFO The primary earnings metric for an equity REIT is AFFO. However, there is a great deal of confusion about what AFFO stands for. The term is “adjusted funds from operations”, but there are considerable differences in which adjustments are being made.
There is a superior way to look at the metric.
We could simply use the FFO with a few standardized adjustments. In this method, we would simply be normalizing the FFO. The major area to normalize is usually the gain or loss on extinguishment of debt.
Buying on multiples The beauty of using normalized FFO is it gets us much closer to a comparable metric. If one REIT has a high dividend yield and the another has a low dividend yield, the normalized FFO multiple should be very helpful. For instance, some investors believe that the large apartment REITs are too expensive. They look at the dividend yields and believe it is too low for a REIT.
They are wrong.
The major apartment REITs are Mid-America Apartment Communities ( MAA ), Essex Property Trust ( ESS ), Equity Residential ( EQR ), UDR ( UDR ), Camden Property Trust ( CPT ), AIMCO ( AIV ), and AvalonBay ( AVB ). These REITs have lower dividend yields than many of their peers, but they are not more expensive. These REITs payout a smaller portion of their FFO so they can continue to expand the portfolio.
Each year, you can expect these apartment REITs to have a slight increase in the number of apartments they own. Consequently, the investor's dividend growth is higher than it would be from only having rental rate increases. Each time another apartment building is added to the REIT, they have another source of income for growing the dividends.
All else equal, the investor would prefer to be paying a smaller earnings multiple. Remember that for equity REITs, earnings means normalized FFO.
Earnings multiples across different types of REITs Some sectors trade at much lower multiples than others. The data center REITs tend to command some of the highest multiples. Simply using an earnings multiple to compare a data center REIT like Equinix ( EQIX ) or CoreSite Realty Corporation ( COR ) to a mall REIT like Simon Property Group ( SPG ) or Taubman Centers ( TCO ) would not be a direct comparison.
The real estate within the REIT may trade at different valuations. A mall REIT is usually going to trade at a lower multiple than a data center REIT. A strip center REIT will usually trade at multiples that are relatively comparable to a mall REIT.
The dangerous impacts of leverage Even within a subsector such as mall REITs, there is a clear difference between the REITs. SPG and TCO trade at higher multiples. Macerich ( MAC ) and General Growth Properties ( GGP ) also command higher multiples compared to the smaller mall REITs.
The mall REIT with the most leverage is CBL Properties ( CBL ). Their excessive debt has caused substantial problems for the REIT. They chose to reduce their common dividend. The yield is still substantial, but the debt was the major problem. The company trades at a very low multiple of normalized FFO, but it has a few major challenges.
The first is the excessive leverage which is increasing their interest costs.
The second is the declining net operating income from their properties. Effectively, each year, on average, the properties are contributing slightly less to FFO. That is a very dangerous sign.
The third problem is that the REIT needs an enormous amount of cash flow for redeveloping properties to bring in new tenants and paying leasing commissions. Given all of these challenges, CBL trades at an extremely low multiple of FFO. The market is correct to give CBL the lowest normalized FFO multiple among the well-known REITs.
Excessive leverage has more than one negative impact on the REIT.
It requires the REIT to pay a higher rate of interest due to the additional risk for the creditors.
It can also force the REIT to sell assets at the worst possible times. For instance, the great recession led to some terrible property sales. Many REITs took significant unrealized losses on the value of their real estate and turned them into realized losses. They were forced to sell precisely when they would’ve wanted to buy. Because this is a major factor that dramatically influences returns over the long haul, investors should demand much lower multiples on REITs with excessive leverage.
Boosting the portfolio yield When an investor is building their portfolio of reliable dividend income, they will still want to diversify their holdings. For instance, many retirees on Seeking Alpha like Procter & Gamble ( PG ), Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ), Pepsi ( PEP ), Coke ( KO ), Altria Group ( MO ), Philip Morris ( PM ), and Apple ( AAPL ).
Investors who want a higher dividend yield can combine preferred shares with their positions in equity REITs.
For investors interested in The REIT Forum’s preferred share ratings, see my guide to preferred shares . I also have a guide for preferred share dividend captures .
The mortgage REIT preferred shares are exceptionally attractive. They offer much higher dividend yields, but many of the portfolios are filled with liquid securities. It can be a time-consuming process to sell a mall or an office building. However, on Wall Street, it is easy to move $1 billion in agency mortgage-backed securities in a day. The liquidity of these portfolios means the mortgage REITs are dramatically safer than they would appear from looking at the common stocks.
There are still a few higher yielding equity REITs that can reasonably be included for a solid dividend. For instance, Tanger Factory Outlets ( SKT ) and Brixmor Property Group ( BRX ) both have high yields but still have solid dividend coverage.
On the preferred side of the equation, we can see much safer dividend yields from CIM-A and CIM-B compared to the common stock of Chimera Investment Corporation ( CIM ). Investors will often find the preferred shares of mortgage REITs carry materially lower dividend yields than the common shares. This reflects the dramatically lower level of risk in the preferred shares. Many investors have simply refused to own preferred shares because they think if the common yield isn’t perfectly safe then the preferred share must be terrible.
They are wrong.
It would be entirely reasonable for an investor to buy a bond from McDonald’s ( MCD ) even if they felt the common stock was too expensive. The ability of the company to cover their fixed costs is not in jeopardy simply because the common stock is richly valued.
Ratings SKT and AVB are 2 of the REITs that are very attractively valued. Both deserve fresh buy ratings.
